html:
A film festival held in Tunis since 1966, the oldest in Africa and the Arab world. Its name recalls ancient Carthage, whose ruins lie at the edge of the city.

It was founded by the critic Tahar Cheriaa with the support of the government of Habib Bourguiba, a few years after Tunisia's independence. Its aim was to give African and Arab filmmakers a place to show their work to their own public, outside the circuit of Europe's festivals. Its top prize is the Tanit d'Or, named after the Carthaginian goddess. The first was won by Ousmane Sembène's Black Girl.

For decades it was held every two years, in turn with a theatre festival, and became yearly in 2014. It helped inspire FESPACO in Burkina Faso, founded in 1969, and the two became the main meeting points of African cinema. Its screenings draw large, young crowds and debates on politics and censorship.
